A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CATArena and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices. Shared methods and retained results establish continuity despite the changed title and substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent tournaments, repeated-run analyses, LLM-player comparisons, and ML and multilingual experiments in its main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original game and code-optimization evaluations, feedback ablations, longer evolutionary trajectories, and failure analyses, including Pommerman experiments.

M1.justification: The iterative code-development and peer-feedback loop and agent architectures remain. v2 adds an objective-task execution branch: submissions are evaluated independently using efficiency objectives, with scores, logs and peer solutions returned as feedback (Section 3.2 and Appendix B). This adapts the existing procedure beyond game tournaments.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's four games and their variants, v2 evaluates OIBench algorithm optimization, SWE-Perf repository optimization, an OIBench memory-optimization variant, and Pommerman (Section 3.2; Appendices J and M). The ML track and tabulated Python/JavaScript/Go evaluations already existed in v1.

E2.justification: The six minimal-agent backbones and four commercial systems remain, with names such as CodeX/Codex matched across versions. However, v1's direct LLM-Player controls and associated comparisons disappear. v2 adds a self-reflection-only comparator in Table 4 and an Elo-versus-global-win-rate comparison in Appendix C, substantially changing the control comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 retains the initial-round score as Sbase but replaces mean-gain global learning with OLS-based Sevo and drops the other principal ability metrics. New protocols include seven-round Gomoku/OIBench experiments, withholding peer feedback, five-problem OIBench and five-instance SWE-Perf evaluations, and CodeBLEU similarity analysis. Existing game match settings largely remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled peer-feedback ablation, seven-round saturation analysis, Hold'em convergence and Elo analyses, HTTP-error diagnostics, and a development-log-based learning case study (Sections 4.3-4.4; Appendices B-C, F and I). Pommerman adds a failure analysis. These substantially extend v1's descriptive analyses; the four game action-similarity heatmaps are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.1 states that tournament metrics average four runs; v2 explicitly reports single-chain main experiments while retaining four repetitions of Rounds 1-2 for stability analysis. This changes documented replication without establishing which experiments were rerun. SWE-Perf additionally introduces 20 test repetitions, three warmups and Mann-Whitney U testing at p<0.1 (Appendices A-B).

E6.justification: Learning results are replaced under the new metric: Claude's Gomoku G.L. is -0.447 in v1 Table 4, whereas Sevo is +0.030 in v2 Table 2; this is not a same-metric performance gain. Optimization, ablation, long-horizon and failure results are added, while LLM-player and decomposed-learning tables disappear. ML, multilingual and original game-cost values are retained.

T1.justification: v1 defines global learning as average improvement over Round 1; v2 Equation 3 defines evolutionary capability as the fitted slope of global performance against round number. v2 also extends scoring to objective-task scalars and omits the explicit counter-adaptation, self-improvement and generalizability formulas, despite residual appendix references. This substantially revises the measurement formalism; no new proofs are supplied.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes an unsaturated game benchmark and the distinction between strategy coding and direct LLM reasoning. v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion center evolutionary capability, claim its first formalization for code agents and independence from initial proficiency, and highlight difficulty combining self-reflection with peer-learning. These redefine the headline contributions.

C2.justification: v1 describes commercial agents as stronger learners; v2 Section 4.2 interprets their advantage as primarily static generation. New explanations connect oscillations to unreliable self-evaluation, distinguish objective-task divergence from game convergence, and identify inadequate initial solutions as barriers to evolution in ML and Pommerman. These materially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability limits.

D1.justification: Generation defaults, fallback models and the game, ML and multilingual prompts largely remain. v2 adds objective-task budgets, execution settings and resource costs, discloses HTTP-error fallback actions, and changes project/code access pointers. It omits v1 Appendix E.3's description of sampling 80-100 intermediate game positions.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward software evolution and continuous code optimization. v2 adds references including Bennett, code-generation evaluations, OIBench and SWE-Perf, while removing much of the discussion of ZeroSumEval, GAMEBot, lmgame-Bench and other game/general-agent benchmarks. Section 2 also introduces an explicit first-to-assess-code-agent-evolution claim.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, framework exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around four research questions, and appendices are reordered and expanded from A-K to A-O. The narrative consistently shifts from general learning abilities toward evolutionary capability.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text, redraws Figure 1, replaces dense multi-ability leaderboards with colored Sbase/Sevo tables, and separates standard and variant results. Agent specifications move to the appendix. New trajectory, ablation, similarity, stability, error and Pommerman displays substantially reshape the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The objective-task evaluations address v1's explicit four-game limitation, while feedback ablations, longer trajectories and error diagnostics strengthen investigation of learning behavior. These gains are tempered by v2's single-chain main results, compared with v1's stated four-run averages, and new reporting inconsistencies: Appendix K claims five-language results although Table 12 retains only Python, JavaScript and Go. The revision offers a limited net improvement in evidential breadth and diagnostic value.
